description:
We are a team of four members from the ACM Student Chapter Huancayo, passionate about software development, data science, and space exploration. For NASA Space Apps 2026.

We combine software engineering, data analysis, and creativity to turn satellite data into meaningful insights. We value collaboration, experimentation, and building technology with real-world impact.
summary: NinaCal (MODIS Operandi) harmonizes NASA FIRMS Aqua/MODIS and Suomi-NPP/VIIRS active-fire detections into one detected-hotspot-day scale from 2003 to 2025 on a 0.05° grid. A public globe console lets anyone search 153 live countries and their regions, scrub or loop the timeline, inspect a year × month calendar and anomalies, compare any two places on one scale, and export CSV. A read-only C++/SQLite API serves the data; a Python pipeline derives satellite availability from daily observations, calibrates MODIS to the VIIRS scale and validates out of sample. Context layers from Microsoft Planetary Computer and Meteomatics add land cover, burned area and daily weather. The project is open source and runs on a static frontend. It states its limits clearly: a thermal hotspot is not a confirmed fire. Coverage is 153 countries, each validated out of sample.
details:
What it does. NinaCal turns six disagreeing satellite fire files into one comparable calendar. Open it and you land on a globe of 153 countries; pick a country, an ADM1 region or draw a box, and the console shows detected hotspot-days per 0.05° cell and month from 2003 to 2025. You can scrub or play the timeline, read a year × month heatmap that keeps estimated months and unavailable source coverage visible, see whether the latest month is unusual against the same month in previous years (median, robust z, and how many previous years it exceeded), compare two countries or regions on one absolute or indexed scale, add land cover, burned area and weather context, and export the current selection as CSV. There is no account and no onboarding.

How it works. A Python pipeline downloads NASA FIRMS country files, aggregates daily detections into monthly cell counts, assigns cells to ADM1 units, and fits a per-cell/per-block calibration from Aqua/MODIS to the Suomi-NPP scale. A NOAA-20 bridge covers months where a sensor really lacks most of its days; availability comes from the daily observation caches, not from a static outage list, and model selection is bias-aware for low-activity countries. Validation is out of sample: fit 2013–2017, development 2018–2020, held-out 2021–2022, drift check 2023–2025. The chosen model and its error are stored per country and shown inside the app: Brazil 6.3% cross-validated WAPE, Australia 4.7%, Peru 13%, while a low-activity country such as Germany reaches 59% — and the console shows that number next to its bias and sample size instead of hiding it. The bundle holds 57.3 million monthly cell rows over 2.79 million 0.05° cells. A C++20 API reads a SQLite database and serves grids, region aggregates, series and CSV behind an Nginx cache; the static Next.js frontend caches every response in IndexedDB, so a second timeline loop makes no network requests. The country catalogue is read from the API at runtime, so adding a country does not require a frontend release.

Mathematical foundation. The conversion is a hierarchically shrunk block-by-quarter ratio, r_b = (Σ_b V + κ r0) / (Σ_b A + κ) and r_b,q = (Σ V + κ r_b) / (Σ A + κ) with κ = 200, applied as min(days in month, r · Aqua cell-days). It is linear in the Aqua count, so any drawn region is the sum of its cells — which is what makes a polygon query possible. Nine candidates compete per country and the winner is chosen on 2018–2020 across five spatial scales, then frozen before the 2021–2022 evaluation. Uncertainty bands are not Poisson: the residual is scaled by sqrt(p + 1 + φp²), with φ estimated on out-of-fold residuals, because naive Poisson bands covered 3 of 8 national months in Peru and 0 of 8 in the United States; the overdispersed scale restores 80–82% nested coverage. Country-level monthly error is 13.3% for Peru and 8.9% for the United States, 23.7% and 21.4% for administrative units, and 47.6% and 58.3% for 0.5° tiles, so the app warns that small regions are noisier than departments or countries. The method, equations and the 78-country evaluation are in the accompanying paper; the live bundle applies the same frozen design to 153 countries, where the app reports each country's own held-out error.

Benefits and impact. Researchers, journalists, agencies and students can compare places and years without rebuilding a harmonization stack, and the same question works at any scale: Peru's 2024 was 25% above its 2003–2024 typical year, Bolivia's +32%, Australia's October 2025 +43% over a typical October, Brazil's October 2025 −34%. Because every country is on one scale, a national agency can put its own season beside a neighbour's without exporting anything. The app is a static frontend, works with no account, is fast after the first load, and keeps the source and the uncertainty visible.

Tools. Next.js, React, TypeScript and MapLibre GL JS for the static frontend on Vercel; C++20, SQLite, Docker and Nginx for the read-only API on a Linux VPS; Python, NumPy and Pandas for the pipeline; Microsoft Planetary Computer (IO land cover, MCD64A1 burned area) and Meteomatics for context; geoBoundaries ADM1 and Natural Earth for boundaries.

Creativity. The globe, the 0.05° country-masked cells, playback served from the browser cache, any-country comparison with an indexed scale, and the land-cover/burned-area/weather context are combined in one instrument rather than a dashboard of disconnected charts. The unusual part is scope: a harmonization that usually stops at one country runs here for 153, with the same method, the same validation and the same caveats in every one of them.

Factors considered. Sensor disagreement and the 2012 seam; sparse data versus true zero; real outage months; low-activity countries where WAPE is unstable and a bias-corrected model is preferable to a lower point error; the difference between a thermal hotspot, a fire and burned area; accessibility and low-bandwidth use; attribution; and the cost of large payloads, which is why the API caps grid and export sizes and the frontend caches instead of re-downloading.

A closing note · Una nota final

"We are a way for the cosmos to know itself." — Carl Sagan, Cosmos (1980).

"Somos una forma que tiene el cosmos de conocerse a sí mismo." — Carl Sagan, Cosmos (1980).

Twenty-three years of satellite detections are, in the end, the record of a planet learning to watch its own fires; NinaCal exists so that record stays comparable, readable and honest about what it cannot see.

Veintitrés años de detecciones satelitales son, al final, el registro de un planeta que aprende a mirar sus propios incendios; NinaCal existe para que ese registro siga siendo comparable, legible y honesto sobre lo que no puede ver.

Acknowledgments · Agradecimientos

We thank the NASA FIRMS and EOSDIS teams, and the MODIS and VIIRS instrument and science teams, for open data and for publishing the outage notices that make an honest record possible. Thanks to the NASA Space Apps organizers, local leads and mentors; to Microsoft Planetary Computer, Meteomatics, geoBoundaries and Natural Earth, OpenStreetMap contributors and Esri for the context layers; and to the maintainers of Next.js, React, MapLibre GL JS, SQLite, Nginx, Docker, NumPy and Pandas, whose work carries projects like this one. Thanks also to the people who opened the console, broke it, and told us. Any remaining error is ours.

Agradecemos a los equipos de NASA FIRMS y EOSDIS, y a los equipos de instrumento y ciencia de MODIS y VIIRS, por los datos abiertos y por publicar los avisos de interrupción que hacen posible un registro honesto. Gracias a los organizadores, leads locales y mentores de NASA Space Apps; a Microsoft Planetary Computer, Meteomatics, geoBoundaries y Natural Earth, a los colaboradores de OpenStreetMap y a Esri por las capas de contexto; y a quienes mantienen Next.js, React, MapLibre GL JS, SQLite, Nginx, Docker, NumPy y Pandas, cuyo trabajo sostiene proyectos como este. Gracias también a quienes abrieron la consola, la rompieron y nos lo dijeron. Cualquier error que quede es nuestro.

On a personal note · En lo personal

To our families, and to the person each of us goes home to: thank you for the hours we borrowed, for the dinners that went cold, and for the patience you gave without being asked. You kept the world running while we stared at pixels; this belongs to you as much as to us.

A nuestras familias y a la persona con la que cada uno vuelve a casa: gracias por las horas que les quitamos, por las cenas que se enfriaron y por la paciencia que nos dieron sin que la pidieran. Ustedes sostuvieron el mundo mientras nosotros mirábamos píxeles; esto también es de ustedes.
